newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Hanoi says on track to achieve economic targets.
newsitem.headline: Hanoi says on track to achieve economic targets.

text.p: Vietnam said on Friday it was on track to reach or surpass most of its economic targets for 1996, but officials indicated concern over a range of problems including trade.

A 25-page statement released ahead of next week's opening of the autumn National Assembly session said lawmakers would be told the country's socio-economic situation had seen continued positive changes in the first nine months of the year.

The statement said Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth would reach 9.5 percent, industrial production 14 percent and inflation would stay below seven percent, while rice output would exceed a 28 million tonne target by 200,000 tonnes.

But in a rare joint news briefing for foreign and domestic journalists, National Assembly spokesman Vu Mao said some "economic issues remain very critical" and pointed to a yawning trade gap and problems with mobilising capital for business.

He said reforms to Vietnam's administrative system were essential and added that the current situation in which banks face a capital surplus while business needs money for investment "should not be allowed".
Vietnam's trade gap soared to more than $3.5 billion in the first nine months of 1996 with imports worth $8.012 billion and exports of $4.475 billion. The total 1995 deficit was $2.3 billion.
At the same time a slight slowdown in the rate of industrial production growth is being accompanied by problems for domestic businesses with acquiring capital for investment.

Finance Minister Ho Te told the briefing that despite the problems, Hanoi was on track to meet economic targets outlined for 1996 and targets in a five-year plan the National Assembly was expected to formally approve at the coming session.

He said the 1996 budget deficit would reach a level equivalent to 3.5 percent of GDP compared with a level last year of 4.3 percent. He added that despite problems with tax collection the gap between revenue and spending was decreasing.
The International Monetary Fund has said that by its system of measurement, Hanoi's stated 4.3 percent deficit is equal to 1.7 percent of GDP.
